title: Beyond WEIRD: The Persistence of Limited Samples and Overgeneralisation in Psychological Science (preprint)
description: Psychological research has been overwhelmingly restricted to WEIRD (Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic) countries making up only approximately 12% of the world's population. Moreover, despite documented cultural differences in things such as brain organisation, most psychological researchers tend to overgeneralise their conclusions beyond WEIRD samples.  In essence whilst there has been an increasing awareness of these issues involving WEIRD dominance and overgeneralisation, it remains unknown whether improvements are occurring in key psychological journals. The focus of this study was to examine the more recent state of affairs regarding: (i) who participates in psychological research? (ii) what demographic factors tend to be reported and/or analysed? and (iii) are findings overgeneralised beyond the samples used? We investigated 45 published papers totalling 133 studies in the journal Psychological Science between June to December 2023 (6 volumes). Samples are still overwhelmingly WEIRD (85%), culturally relevant characteristics are reported no more than half the time (i.e., 54% in abstracts and 26% in relevance statements), statistically analysed a third of the time (33%), and overgeneralisations occur nearly all the time (i.e., 97% in abstracts and 94% in relevance statements and discussions). Despite increasing attention to the WEIRD problem and overgeneralisation, their persistence remains. More urgency is required, and suggestions are offered for going forward. Improving sample diversity and reducing overgeneralisations matters if we are to understand how human minds work across the planet.

title: „Die KI wird’s schon richten“ – Eine psychologische Perspektive auf Automation Bias und richterliche Unabhängigkeit
description: Dieser Beitrag beschreibt das Phänomen des Automation Bias aus psychologischer Perspektive. Automation Bias wird in der Verordnung zur Festlegung harmonisierter Vorschriften für Künstliche Intelligenz (KI-Verordnung, KI-VO) in Artikel 14 Abs. b) und in vielen Debatten zum Einsatz von Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) in Hochrisikobereichen vor allem als Phänomen des übermäßigen Vertrauens dargestellt. Diese Darstellung wird jedoch der Komplexität des Phänomens kaum gerecht. Basierend auf psychologischer Literatur stellen wir Automation Bias als ein Phänomen dar, das mit Aufmerksamkeits- und Vertrauensprozessen sowie mit gefühlter Verantwortlichkeit zusammenhängt. Zugleich beschreiben dieser Beitrag technische, menschliche und kontextuelle Einflussfaktoren auf diese psychologischen Prozesse, welche die Wahrscheinlichkeit von Automation Bias verstärken oder abschwächen können. Im letzten Teil des Beitrages stellen wir die Beziehung zwischen den psychologischen Perspektiven des Automation Bias und der richterlichen Unabhängigkeit her.

title: Association between Anomalous Subjective Recall and Long-Range Temporal Correlations in Resting-State EEG: An Individual-Differences Study of Depersonalization Tendency
description: Anomalous subjective recall refers to autobiographical memories whose factual content can be retrieved but are not experienced as one’s own, instead feeling alien. It is thought to reflect disrupted temporal self-continuity during depersonalization; however, its neural basis remains poorly understood. Because task-based measures may be less suitable for capturing trait-like alterations in neural dynamics, resting-state electroencephalography may provide a useful marker of such disturbances. We examined whether higher levels of anomalous subjective recall are associated with lower alpha-band long-range temporal correlations. Eighty-one healthy adults completed the Japanese Cambridge Depersonalization Scale and underwent 5 minutes of eyes-closed resting-state electroencephalography. Alpha-band long-range temporal correlations were quantified at FCz using the detrended fluctuation analysis exponent. We tested the hypothesis that higher anomalous subjective recall would be associated with lower values, controlling for age, sex, body mass index, and the number of artifact-free epochs. Anomalous subjective recall showed a significant negative partial Spearman correlation with the detrended fluctuation analysis exponent at FCz. In a multiple regression model including anomalous subjective recall and other depersonalization dimensions, the coefficient for anomalous subjective recall remained negative but was not statistically significant. These findings provide preliminary correlational evidence that reduced temporal integration in frontocentral alpha-band activity may be associated with subjective disconnection from autobiographical memories, although evidence for symptom-level specificity remains limited.

title: The Social Indicating Response (SIR): An Operational Definition for Assent-Based Mand Training Within Interrupted Play-Chain Episodes
description: Indicating responses (IRs) — rudimentary communicative behaviors evoked by an establishing operation — have been described in the behavior-analytic and SLP literatures for decades and were recently formalized as a tutorial construct by Frampton, Axe, Davis, Meleshkevich, and Li (2024). The present paper introduces and operationalizes a refinement of the IR construct: the Social Indicating Response (SIR). An SIR is a cluster of two or more rudimentary indicating-response topographies — at least one of which is socially directed — emitted via initiation by the learner or within a 5-s window during the programmed delay of an interrupted play-chain episode, that appears to function as a social mand for the instructor to continue, modify, or terminate the chain — resulting in delivery of an item, action, or social attention, or continuation, modification, or termination of the chain. The SIR construct was first published in operational form by the present author in the K&K Sign/Select to Talk Treatment Manual (Kasper & Kaufman, 2025, Northern Speech Services, pp. 10–11) and was developed across earlier invited presentations (Kasper, 2022; Kasper & degli Espinosa, 2022). The SIR is a core dependent measure for the present author’s line of changing-criterion-design (CCD) studies on assent-based play-chain training, with public introduction at the 52nd Annual Convention of the Association for Behavior Analysis International (Kasper, 2026, Workshop PBID #15, San Francisco, CA).

title: Bayesian Predictive Ensembles for Random Effects Specification Uncertainty: Capturing Individual Heterogeneity in Large-Scale Assessments
description: A common challenge in multilevel modeling is determining which predictors should have random effects, especially in educational and psychological research where several theoretically plausible model specifications exist. Choosing a single specification ignores information from the alternatives and can lead to understated uncertainty in later inference. Popular Bayesian ensemble methods, including Bayesian model averaging (BMA), Bayesian stacking (BS), and Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS), combine predictions across candidate specifications but constrain model weights to sum to one, implicitly assuming that the candidate model set collectively accounts for all systematic variance in the outcome. This assumption rarely holds when each candidate captures only a portion of the true random effects structure. To address this, we propose to apply the Varying Coefficient Bayesian Additive Regression Tree (VCBART; Deshpande, Bai, Balocchi, Starling, & Weiss, 2024) with an adaptive intercept that absorbs variance not captured by any candidate model. The approach estimates individual-specific ensemble weights as nonparametric functions of individual-level and cluster-level covariates without imposing a sum-to-one constraint. The posterior distributions of these weights indicate which random-effects structures are most relevant for each individual and quantify the associated uncertainty. We evaluate VCBART using simulations calibrated to the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018 mathematics data and an empirical application to the same data. Among the methods compared, VCBART achieves near-nominal prediction interval coverage with the lowest prediction error. It even outperforms the correctly specified oracle in out-of-sample prediction under high within-cluster variability.

title: Stereotypes as Byproducts of Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
description: Stereotypes are ubiquitous even when inaccurate. Why do they arise readily and persist? We propose a novel computational account linking person perception and group stereotypes: stereotypes emerge as byproducts of hierarchical Bayesian inference (HBI), which aims to maximize the accuracy of person perception. While efficient for individual-level perception, HBI can facilitate biased group stereotypes. We tested and supported four stereotype-related predictions derived from HBI using five simulations and seven empirical samples (n = 1,273). Consistent with HBI, stereotypes not only emerged when perceivers were asymmetrically exposed to different groups (Study 1) but also when exposure was sufficient, because HBI enables faster acquisition of group-level impressions (Study 2). Established group beliefs persisted because counterevidence was attributed to idiosyncrasies (Study 3) or to an individual's secondary group membership (Study 4). Together, these findings suggest HBI as a unifying account of stereotypes, advancing a generalizable computational framework for social cognition.

title: mpathic Psychologist-led AI Clinical Tests Suicide Benchmark (mPACT-S-v1.0)
description: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for emotional support and mental health guidance, including in conversations that may involve suicide-related risk. Existing evaluation approaches often rely on automated users or LLM-based judges and may not adequately capture clinically meaningful distinctions among detection, risk interpretation, and response generation. We developed the mpathic Psychologist-led AI Clinical Tests Suicide Benchmark (mPACT-S-v1.0), a clinician-developed benchmark for evaluating LLM behavior in simulated suicide-related conversations. Licensed clinicians authored 300 multi-turn roleplays across four C-SSRS-informed risk levels and evaluated model responses using a multi-label framework capturing helpful, less harmful, and more harmful behaviors. Six LLMs were evaluated in default API configurations. Models varied substantially on the severity-weighted mPACT-S score, with Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5.2 achieving the highest scores and Grok 4.1 and Mistral Medium 3 scoring lowest. Models were generally more successful at avoiding harmful responses than at producing actively helpful ones, and the relationship between harm avoidance and clinically appropriate responding varied across systems. These findings suggest that suicide-related LLM evaluation requires clinician-guided, risk-sensitive benchmarks that assess both harmful response avoidance and active, clinically appropriate support.

title: Exploring Psychological Trade-offs: Developing and Demonstrating an R Shiny App for Pareto Optimization
description: While some are neutral, many psychological constructs (e.g., depression, learning motivation, or antisocial behavior) carry clear directional expectations that align with social or ethical principles and values. When a construct is framed with the goal of moving toward its socially desirable direction, it becomes a meaningful psychological objective to pursue. We pursue different objectives in our daily lives, sometimes simultaneously. During this process, trade-offs occur when they are in tension or conflict, meaning they cannot be consistently improved without compromising one another. While certain psychological trade-offs have been well studied, others remain underexplored or possibly even unidentified. One critical reason is that mainstream analytic methods used in psychological research are not designed to investigate such trade-offs. Fortunately, a suitable method has long existed in other disciplines. Pareto Optimization (PO) is an effective analytic framework widely applied in fields such as biology, economics, and engineering to investigate trade-offs among multiple competing objectives. In this tutorial, we review the core conceptual and methodological foundations of PO and aim to bring this classic method to a psychological audience. Moreover, we develop a user-friendly R Shiny application (named PO-Run) for conducting PO analyses. The utility of the application is illustrated through a real-world psychological example that simultaneously pursues two conflicting objectives: promoting critical actions and minimizing mental stress. Their trade-off relationship is then evaluated via the evidence generated by PO-Run, along with relevant theoretical justification.

title: mpathic Psychologist-led AI Clinical Tests Eating Disorders Benchmark (mPACT-ED-v1.0)
description: The mpathic Psychologist-led AI Clinical Tests Eating Disorders Index (mPACT-ED-v1.0) benchmark is a comparison of large language models (LLM) in their response to mental health content involving disordered eating presentations. Eating disorders are among the most lethal psychiatric conditions, yet standardized benchmarks for evaluating AI conversations in this domain remain scarce, limiting rigorous cross-system comparison, harm potential, and measurement of improvement over time. Developed with clinicians, mPACT-ED-v1.0 comprises realistic, clinician-authored, multi-turn scenarios spanning a range of disordered eating presentations, from subclinical symptoms to severe and high-vulnerability profiles. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on LLM-generated users or automated evaluation, this benchmark uses exclusively human, clinician-generated conversations and evaluation to ensure alignment with established clinical standards. Specifically, mPACT-ED-v1.0 assesses whether models generate non-reinforcing, clinically calibrated, risk-responsive responses.  Conversation-level mPACT-ED Composite scores reflect the mean talk-turn score normalized to a 0–10 scale where higher scores indicate a more appropriate response (i.e., similar to how a human clinician would respond). Across all evaluated conversations, models varied in their overall severity-weighted mPACT-ED scores with ranges between 7.12 (Claude) and 6.22 (Grok 4.1), representing a gap of approximately 0.90 points between the highest and lowest performers. mPACT-ED-v1.0 was designed to support developers measuring model improvements, regulators verifying system performance, and researchers and clinicians studying AI behavior in both consumer and high-vulnerability mental health contexts. As a focused eating disorder clinician benchmark for AI, mPACT-ED-v1.0 provides a rigorous framework for evaluating whether AI systems can support users appropriately while avoiding harmful or escalating responses.

title: Autonomy Support and Controlling Parenting in Tanzania: A Mixed-Methods Examination of Structure and Cultural Meaning among Parents of Young Children
description: Objective: Parental autonomy support and controlling parenting are central constructs in developmental science, yet their structural organization and contextual meanings remain underexamined in sub-Saharan African contexts. This study investigated these dimensions among Tanzanian parents of young children using a complementary mixed-methods design. Design: A total of 204 parents of children aged below 8 years completed the Perceived Parental Autonomy Support Scale (P-PASS), and a subsample of 16 parents participated in semi-structured interviews. Results: Confirmatory factor analyses indicated that the original two-factor structure did not fully replicate. However, exploratory structural equation modeling and exploratory factor analyses supported a broadly interpretable two-dimensional structure with limited cross-loadings. Autonomy support and controlling parenting were moderately and positively correlated (r = .51), with no significant differences across parental sex and modest variation across districts for autonomy support. Qualitative findings showed that parents conceptualized autonomy primarily in terms of responsibility, self-management, and adherence to socially valued roles, often embedded within structured and adult-directed practices. Controlling and punitive strategies were frequently described as means of fostering discipline, reflecting parental representations rather than evidence of developmental effectiveness. Conclusions: Overall, the findings suggest that autonomy-related constructs retain broad relevance while their differentiation and interpretation may vary across contexts, highlighting the importance of culturally sensitive measurement and the distinction between autonomy-supportive structure and controlling practices.

title: AI Use, Disclosure, and Training Across School-Based and Related Service Professionals in Ohio
description:
Objective:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across healthcare and education professions, yet cross-professional evidence on adoption and governance practices remains limited. This study examined differences across allied health and related service professionals in AI use, disclosure practices, beliefs about informed consent, and training experiences.
Methods:
Participants were 1,350 allied health and related service professionals practicing in Ohio, including physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech-language pathologists, school psychologists, counselors, nurses, and assistant-level providers. The survey was adapted from prior school psychology AI studies and refined with multidisciplinary task force input. Analyses examined differences across professional roles in frequency of AI use, disclosure practices, informed consent beliefs, and type of AI training received. Missing data were addressed using multiple imputation.
Results:
AI use differed significantly across professional roles, with school psychologists, counselors, and speech-language pathologists reporting the highest levels of use, and occupational therapy assistants and physical therapy assistants reporting the lowest. Disclosure practices also varied significantly, with school psychologists and speech-language pathologists reporting greater disclosure than several other groups. Differences in informed consent practices were statistically significant but small, with school psychologists, counselors, and speech-language pathologists somewhat more likely to report obtaining consent, and assistants and nurses somewhat more likely to report not obtaining consent. Training disparities were pronounced: school psychologists, counselors, and speech-language pathologists were more likely to report formal AI training, whereas assistants were substantially more likely to report no AI training.

title: How well does the literature on behavioral interventions generalize? An empirical test
description: In the social and behavioral sciences, research syntheses represent our most established method for producing generalizable knowledge from scientific literature. Yet whether syntheses do in fact produce generalizable knowledge is rarely empirically tested. In this paper, we propose a formal test of generalizability: a research synthesis produces generalizable knowledge to the extent that it can predict the results of new studies. To demonstrate this approach, we train machine learning models on each of three distinct syntheses of the literature on behavior change interventions (containing collectively 711 experiments). We then evaluate how well each model predicts the effect sizes of studies it has not yet seen—i.e., studies from one of the other syntheses. Synthesis-to-synthesis predictions outperform naive benchmarks (i.e., models that simply predict the average effect size) but provide only limited practical guidance on intervention effectiveness. We examine model and feature characteristics to explain why, tracing their roots to two field-level challenges: sampling bias in synthesis construction and measurement error in study documentation. We argue that knowledge cannot generalize across varied studies if variations are not consistently captured. Cumulation requires ex-ante coordination.

title: The association between fine motor deficits and difficulties in reading, language, and mathematics is mediated by lower general intelligence
description: Fine motor skills have been investigated as a potential marker of neurodevelopmental functioning. Previous studies investigating the link between fine motor skills and reading, language, and mathematical difficulties have reported inconsistent findings. Some studies suggested the potential role of general cognitive abilities in mediating these associations, but systematic evaluations of this hypothesis have not been conducted. We analysed performance on four fine motor tasks, including pegboard, marking squares, sorting matches, and threading laces in children from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children cohort (ALSPAC). Children with reading difficulties (RD; N = 144), language difficulties (LD; N = 152), mathematical difficulties (MD; N = 102), and co-occurrence of two or more of these difficulties (N = 104) performed worse in fine motor skills compared to typically developing controls (TD; N = 786). However, after controlling for sex and IQ, no statistically significant group differences in fine motor skills were found. Logistic regression analyses showed that IQ was the most robust and consistent predictor distinguishing the difficulty groups from TD, whereas fine motor skills contributed minimally. Subsequent mediation analyses showed that IQ mediated the relationship between fine motor skills and group status. These findings suggest that the association between fine motor skills and reading, language and mathematical difficulties is not specific to these domains but appears mediated by lower general cognitive ability.

title: A Five-Dimensional Neural Model for Precision Psychiatry: From a Single Neuron to a Complex Interactive System
description: Current psychiatric classification systems are still largely based on symptom clusters. Although clinically useful, they often do not explain the underlying mechanisms that generate those symptoms. This article presents the Five-Dimensional Neural Model for Precision Psychiatry (5DNM), a framework grounded in contemporary neuroscience and designed to support individualized clinical reasoning. The model conceptualizes psychiatric presentations through five interrelated dimensions of the same integrated system: (1) Neuronal States and Circuit Functions (D1; micro-level), (2) Brain Networks and Functional Connectivity (D2; meso-level), (3) Global Brain Activity and Modes (D3; macro-level, state), (4) Information Processing (external–internal–integrative) (D4; macro-level, computational), and (5) Self (self-awareness, volition, self-control) and Interpersonal Processes (D5; meta-level, experiential). These are not separate parts of the system, but different ways of examining the same system at different levels of organization. The article also introduces a practical clinical method — Mapping–Formulation–Navigation (MFN) — for applying the model in case formulation and treatment planning. Taken together, 5DNM and MFN are intended to support mechanism-based, individualized psychiatric formulation and care. Two simulated case examples, generated with the aid of a prototype AI-based support tool, are also provided to illustrate how the five-dimensional model links clinical data to neurobiological levels of organization, and how the MFN workflow translates this mapping into provisional mechanistic formulations and sequenced, monitorable intervention plans.

title: Building language: Mean Length of Utterance, Lexical Growth, and Grammatical Accuracy in Spanish-speaking Monolingual Children
description:
Purpose: This study established age-based reference benchmarks for grammaticality and lexical productivity in monolingual Spanish-speaking children using narrative retell tasks. Developmental changes in Mean Length of Utterance in words (MLUw), Total Number of Words (TNW), Percentage of Grammatical Utterances (PGU), and Moving Average Type-Token Ratio (MATTR) were examined in children aged 3;0–6;11 years.
Method: A cross-sectional quantitative design was used with 819 monolingual Spanish-speaking children recruited from mainstream educational settings. Narrative retell tasks elicited spontaneous language samples, from which MLUw, TNW, PGU, and MATTR were derived. Age-based descriptive and percentile analyses were conducted.
Results: Results showed age-related increases in lexical productivity and grammatical accuracy. TNW increased from 105 words at age 3 to 180 words at age 6. PGU improved from 75% at age 3 to approximately 88–90% at ages 4–6. MATTR remained relatively stable across age groups, ranging from 0.46 to 0.48.
Conclusion: Findings support conceptualising language performance as a developmental continuum and demonstrate the diagnostic utility of percentile-based interpretation. This study provides the first comprehensive reference benchmarks for narrative language measures in monolingual Spanish-speaking children and offers clinically relevant tools for more precise assessment in Spanish-speaking contexts.

title: An unusual cycle of literary translations reveals distinct mechanisms of cultural evolution
description: How do stories change as they cross linguistic and cultural boundaries? Many theories of cultural evolution emphasize the influence of repeated transmission, but in real-world cross-cultural dissemination, transmission is typically confounded with large-scale changes in cultural context. This makes it difficult to identify mechanisms of cultural stability and change. Here, to unravel this theoretical tangle, we leverage an unusual translation cycle: a story first published in English was translated into Russian by novelist Leo Tolstoy, misattributed to Tolstoy, translated into French, and finally translated back into English --- with the first and final versions published in the same language, city (Chicago, USA), and time period (mid-1890s). This unusual 'translation cycle' offers a unique opportunity to separate the cumulative effects of iterated transmission from the influences of the broader cultural context. Using a novel computational method that represents stories as high-dimensional semantic trajectories, we show that each translation introduced cumulative distortions. Strikingly, when the story was translated back into its original cultural context, its semantic trajectory shifted toward the original version, despite the final translator having no knowledge of the original, consistent with a regularizing influence of the shared cultural context. Our findings reveal how the broader cultural context can act as a stabilizing force in cultural evolution, constraining variation introduced by repeated transmission.

title: The Development of Social Reasoning About Shared Sleep Arrangements
description: Shared sleep arrangements, especially children’s, often occur in proximity to family and other caregivers. We investigated whether sleep-sharing serves as a reliable cue to familial and caregiving relationships, even in childhood. Two preregistered studies with U.S. 5–7-year-olds (N = 168) and adults (N = 168) show people possess systematic intuitions about the social meaning of shared sleep arrangements. In Study 1, both age groups robustly expected that a child character sleep-shared with family over non-family (siblings over friends; parents over teachers), while expecting equal toy-sharing. In Study 2, both age groups predicted that a child’s chosen sleep-sharing (vs. toy-sharing) partner would provide physical comfort (care) when the child became upset. Adults privileged sleep-sharing over another intimate interaction––saliva-sharing––as diagnostic of a caregiving relationship. From early childhood, people use shared sleep arrangements as a powerful signal of intimate relationships, supporting their understanding of the social landscape.

title: Cross-Cultural Validation of the Morality-as-Cooperation Questionnaire in Brazil
description: Morality-As-Cooperation provides a framework for understanding how moral behaviors and values are rooted in cooperative social interactions, a fundamental aspect of human evolution. To advance our understanding of moral psychology, particularly to test whether MAC is a universally valid construct, it is important to examine it across different countries and cultures. The present investigation is among the first to extend this theory to Brazil. In Study 1 (N = 223), we translated, adapted, and validated the Morality-As-Cooperation Questionnaire for Brazilian Portuguese, assessing its structural validity, reliability, convergent validity, and measurement invariance with the original U.S. sample. Results showed that the Relevance subscale demonstrated good reliability, model fit, and cross-cultural invariance, whereas the Judgment subscale demonstrated acceptable reliability but weaker and less stable properties. In Study 2 (N = 590), we examined discriminant and concurrent validity using a Brazilian general population sample. The Relevance subscale again demonstrated good reliability and measurement invariance across Brazilian and U.S. samples, whereas the Judgment subscale once more showed acceptable reliability but persistent psychometric instability. Together, these findings suggest that Morality-As-Cooperation offers a useful framework for studying morality in Brazil and beyond, although refinement of the Judgment subscale is needed to ensure robust cross-cultural applications.

title: The relation between processing speed and working memory capacity: No difference across varying procedural working memory demands
description: The binding hypothesis has been proposed as a potential explanation of the observed relation between processing speed (PS) and working memory capacity (WMC). According to this hypothesis, PS and WMC are correlated as both demand WM maintenance. However, past studies showed mixed results for the binding hypothesis as an explanation. Here, we extended this line of work by examining whether correlations between individuals’ PS and WMC are strengthened when procedural WM demands on reconfiguration and protection against proactive interference in PS tasks are high. We compared correlations when high procedural WM demands are afforded as stimulus-response mapping change throughout PS tasks relative to consistent mappings with only one set of mappings throughout PS tasks. Yet, our results show similar correlations between PS and WMC when higher procedural WM demands are implemented questioning whether the binding hypothesis can serve as an explanation for the relation between PS and WMC. However, performance in PS tasks with changing and consistent mapping was highly correlated indicating that factors or processes unaffected by consistencies drive the PS-WMC relation. Future studies should examine whether cue-stimulus intervals, set sizes, or methods to test the binding hypothesis could have mitigated procedural WM demands in PS tasks accounting for the lack of correlational differences.

title: The Coding Brain: P600 Effects Elicited by the Visual Programming Language ScratchJr
description:
In recent years, there is a growing emphasis on early childhood coding education to equip
students with essential skills for an increasingly technical society. While emerging research has
investigated how text-based programming languages are processed in the adult brain, the neural
mechanisms underlying early childhood visual programming languages like ScratchJr remain
largely unexplored. This preregistered study examined the cognitive basis of ScratchJr
processing, with two primary research aims: 1. Investigate whether ScratchJr elicits neural
signatures comparable to natural languages and other rule-based processes (specifically N400
and semantic P600 responses) and 2. Explore how ScratchJr competence modulates these effects.
We recorded event-related potentials (ERPs) from 40 (N = 40) adults while they completed a
semantic congruency task using ScratchJr stimuli. Neural responses were analyzed in time bins
associated with N400 and P600 components, and ScratchJr competence was included as a
potential factor to modulate these results. Results revealed a P600 response to semantic
violations, with no modulation by ScratchJr competence. These findings contribute to a growing
body of literature on the processing of programming languages and support the notion that
ScratchJr processing evokes neural mechanisms related to structured processes such as natural
language.

title: A triadic model of bilingual shared reading:  Contributions of the book, parent, and child in shaping dual language use
description: This study proposes and tests a triadic model of shared reading in bilingual contexts. Sixty-two Spanish-English bilingual parents (92% mothers, 88% Latino) and children (M=3.86 years, 51.6% male) read an English-only Monolingual book and bilingual Codeswitching book with Spanish words embedded in English text. Both parents and children produced more Spanish and codeswitching when sharing Codeswitching vs. Monolingual books, and dyads’ Spanish use was positively correlated while reading both books. These findings reveal that books, parents, and children all make meaningful contributions to the learning opportunities available during shared reading, consistent with the proposed triadic model. This framework can inform a deeper understanding of shared reading interactions that include diverse language experiences and environments.

title: Sensitivity Analysis of Computational Models in Psychology: A Tutorial
description: There has been an increasing interest in formal models in psychology, allowing researchers to betterunderstand and intervene on psychological systems. However, the methods and tools for understandingand analysing these models are rarely used in psychological research. This is not necessarily due to a lackof methodology, but rather due to them not being familiar in this field. This paper introduces one suchmethod from computational science that can be used to determine the influence of model parameterson an output variable: (global) Sensitivity Analysis (SA). We first discuss the main goals of an SA andpotential applications, such as determining which parameters are the most relevant for causing a changein a chosen model output, such as suicidal thoughts or frequency of panic attacks. We then presenttwo methods that can be used to conduct an SA: the variance-based Sobol SA and the density-basedPAWN. Both of them are demonstrated using an existing computational model in a tutorial-like fashion,provided by (annotated) code in R. The results are connected to empirical literature and implicationsfor model evaluations are discussed. Lastly, we aggregate the entire process into a workflow and codepipeline that can be easily applied to other models. Although this paper only demonstrates the basicapplication of SA, further extensions and purposes, such as model calibration, are discussed.

title: The Behavioral Science Conference Presentations Database
description: Behavioral scientists give thousands of conference talks each year, and these presentations are the field's fastest-circulating record of active research. Yet they have not been systematically indexed. I introduce the Behavioral Science Conference Presentations Database, a public, free-to-use archive that currently spans 73,248 presentations across 21 conference series and 144 individual meetings from 2015 to 2026, with seven search modes and landing pages for each conference, session, topic, and author. The index is at https://www.joesiev.com/conferences. Three descriptive findings illustrate its utility. I first explore three behavioral subfields—consumer research (ACR), social psychology (SPSP), and organizational behavior (AOM-OB)—and document their shifting topic profiles between 2015 and 2025, including the explosion of AI-related papers presented at these meetings. I find that this work has predominantly treated AI as a psychological stimulus, but increasingly uses it as a research tool or method and even as a subject of psychological study itself. I then zoom in on marketing, exploring how topic shares at ACR have shifted between psychological process, marketplace/consumption, social issues, and digital technology. These findings show how research attention shifts within and across subfields over time, highlighting the meta-scientific value of conference programs.

title: Dissociating Sensory and Decision Processes in Tasting: Intensity Affects Sensitivity, while Expectancies and Feedback Interact, Affecting Decision Criteria
description: The aim of this study was to examine the influence of feedback on the dynamics of sensory and decision processes in a tasting task involving mixtures of salty and sour basic tastes. The Double Dissociation Additive Test within the Signal Detection Theory framework was applied to assess the effects of manipulating intensity, signal-noise base rates, and feedback on sensitivity and decision-making processes. Participants’ discrimination improved as salt concentration increased, regardless of induced bias or feedback presence; however, feedback led to a general increase in sensitivity. Both signal-noise stimulus base rates and feedback influenced the decision-making process. When feedback was present, detection judgments aligned more closely with actual signal-noise stimulus base rates. However, in the absence of feedback, the relationship between base rates and response bias reversed. Implications for research in sensory evaluation and perceptual learning are discussed.

title: Measuring Behavioral Avoidance in Misophonia: Development and Validation of the Misophonic Behavioral Avoidance Test (M-BAT)
description: Avoidance is central in selective sound intolerance (misophonia), yet lacks objective behavioral assessment. We present the Misophonic Behavioral Avoidance Test (M-BAT), a standardized computerized task with two subtests to measure reactive (sound endurance) and anticipating avoidance tendency via behavioral indicators and response times (RTs). Different than most behavioral avoidance tests, the M-BAT can be easily applied online to large samples. In a validation study on N = 381 adults with misophonic symptoms, we fitted Bayesian Item Response Theory (IRT) models to endurance times, avoidance indicators and RTs to evaluate reliability, measurement invariance (MI), and several facets of validity. Unidimensional models fitted subtests well with high reliability (ρEAP ≈ .88/.94), and MI across gender, misophonia severity and age was broadly supported, despite localized differential item functioning. Sound endurance and anticipating avoidance tendency were moderately related (r = -.30) and showed theory-consistent, moderate associations with self-reported misophonic symptoms including avoidance, distinguished clinical from subclinical misophonia groups, and predicted everyday behavior (daily escape and prevention). We found little evidence that contextual factors, such as the stimuli presentation or the individuality of stimuli influenced test responses, however, findings demonstrated influences due to participants high test motivation. Challenges in establishing discriminant, internal, and incremental validity remain. Overall, the M-BAT provides reliable, easily applicable, and objective behavioral measures that complement questionnaires and psychoacoustic ratings, supporting clinical research and treatment evaluation.

title: AMPT : A Tool for Personalizing Math Learning with Generative AI
description: We developed the AI Math Personalization Tool (AMPT) to explore how personalization and agency over the contexts in math story problems can affect student learning and motivation for mathematics. AMPT uses a conversational interface to learn about students’ interests before creating a math story problem targeting those interests. Feedback gathered through co-design sessions with AMPT provided insight into areas where agency over the story of the problem was particularly important to students (e.g., naming characters) as well as the contextual topics students find interesting. Further, following AMPT sessions, students’ sense of belonging in mathematics increased. By leveraging generative AI to support personalization at scale, AMPT provides a framework for investigating how agency and representation relate to student engagement in mathematics. These insights have broader implications for the design of AI-driven learning tools and the future of personalized education.

title: A Practical Unified Framework for Evaluating Psychological Theories and Observational Research Practices
description:
In psychology, knowledge advances primarily through theory development and empirical testing within a dominant framework: theory, hypothesis, design, measurement, modeling, and interpretation. Although rigorous execution is assumed to yield valid insights, meta-scientific critiques reveal profound shortcomings. This article addresses these by (1) identifying seven core deficiencies in theory development; (2) delineating seven critical flaws in observational empirical testing; and (3) introducing three coherence dimensions (conceptual, causal, technical) across the pipeline as an integrative requirement. We synthesize these previously fragmented critiques into a novel, unified evaluative framework consisting of 14 explicit evaluation criteria plus three coherence dimensions. For each component we derive concrete, manuscript-level assessment criteria that can be applied at the sentence and section level. We demonstrate the framework’s practical utility by applying it to two published empirical papers, revealing detectable issues even in high-quality work. 
Compounded with well-documented problems such as low statistical power (~36%) and replication rates of 30–50%, these upstream deficiencies likely render a substantial proportion of published findings fragile or uninterpretable. Importantly, these flaws lie upstream of replication: while replication is essential for assessing reproducibility and can motivate theory revision, it cannot remedy deeper theoretical and methodological weaknesses and may, in some cases, reinforce flawed conclusions. By providing a practical tool for structured assessment and reform, this framework aims to strengthen theory construction, empirical rigor, and cumulative progress in psychology and related social sciences.

title: Stealth Assessments in Technology-Rich Learning Environments:  A Systematic Review of Implementation, Modeling, and Psychometric Quality
description: Advances in digital technologies, data logging, and computational modeling increasingly enable unobtrusive, continuous assessment as learners interact with technology-rich environments. Stealth assessment reflects this shift by embedding evidence-based assessment within learning activities to support real-time inference, feedback, and personalization. Following PRISMA guidelines, this systematic review synthesized 161 publications representing 164 study entries published between 2004 and 2026 to examine: (1) where and how stealth assessment has been implemented across environments, populations, competencies, and purposes; and (2) how studies modeled evidence identification and accumulation in relation to psychometric quality, fidelity to evidence-centered design, and validity evidence. Results show expansion beyond games into simulations, intelligent tutoring systems, virtual reality, and applied domains, but continued concentration in K–12 contexts and cognitive or disciplinary competencies. Modeling sophistication varied widely but was not associated with stronger psychometric quality reporting or greater fidelity. Validity evidence was commonly reported, whereas reliability and fairness were rarely addressed.

title: When ‘Right Now’ Isn’t ‘Right Now’: The Elasticity of the Moment(ary) in ESM Studies
description: Recently, Eisele and colleagues (2025) published the ESM-Q, a set of quality criteria for developing and evaluating Experience Sampling Method (ESM) items. While we agree with one of their core recommendations to specify the timeframe an item refers to (e.g., “Right now, I feel happy”), we comment here on how this may be less straightforward than implicitly assumed by ESM researchers. Drawing on our own ESM studies, in which we collected qualitative data from participants, we show that the popular momentary timeframe “right now” is interpreted by participants in different ways, often covering not only the moment just before the assessment but drawing on past, present and anticipated future times. We outline how differences in interpretations can be explained by the linguistic ambiguity of the time adverbs that we use to signify timeframes, as well as by participants’ individual experience of time. We close the commentary with implications on the severity of these differences in interpretation, and provide some concrete recommendations for ESM researchers.

title: Workload and Feedback Immediacy Shape Willingness to Offload Working Memory to AI: Neural evidence
description:
Objective: This study examined how workload and feedback timing influence cognitive offloading to AI systems, using neural measures to track how operators allocate working memory resources between internal processing and external support.

Background: Effective human–AI teaming depends on calibrated trust and appropriate cognitive offloading. However, feedback timing may influence how reliably system performance is learned and how operators distribute cognitive resources during interaction.

Method: In two experiments, participants performed a change-detection task alone (solo blocks) or alongside an AI monitoring half the visual field (dyad blocks). Workload was manipulated within, feedback immediacy (block-wise vs. trial-wise) between participants. The contralateral delay activity (CDA) served as a neural index of working memory maintenance and cognitive offloading.

Results: Dyad blocks produced reduced CDA amplitudes relative to solo blocks, consistent with incomplete offloading to the AI. When feedback was non-immediate (block-wise; Experiment 1), solo-dyad CDA differences were identical under low and high workload, indicating that offloading was not modulated by task demands. When feedback was immediate (trial-wise; Experiment 2), self-reported trust was increased and solo-dyad CDA differences were pronounced under low workload but attenuated under high workload. This indicates that offloading increased specifically when immediate feedback coincided with high task demands, together with higher attitudinal trust.

Conclusion: Offloading increased specifically when immediate feedback and high workload coincided. Neural measures captured internal monitoring processes invisible to behavioral measures alone.

Application: AI systems providing timely, transparent feedback may support calibrated trust and promote efficient cognitive resource allocation in human–AI teaming environment.

title: Sensitive Periods for and Accumulation of Childhood Adversity on Adolescent Development in Ghana
description: Childhood adversity can have profound consequences on adolescents’ cognitive and social-emotional development, yet whether the developmental timing or the accumulation of exposure to these experiences over time is most predictive of unfavorable later-life outcomes remains unclear. This study draws on a longitudinal sample in peri-urban Ghana (N = 1,921; 50.4% girls, all Ghanaian nationals) to examine how children’s exposure to five adversities at ages 5, 6, 7, 8, and 11 predicts outcomes at age 13. We employed the Structured Life Course Modeling Approach (SLCMA) to test whether sensitive periods or accumulation life-course hypotheses most strongly predicted and accounted for variation in adolescent outcomes. Models specifying a sensitive period were better-fitting than accumulation models in predicting adolescent outcomes: physical aggression and household food insecurity at age 11 were the most predictive of lower cognitive and social-emotional outcomes, and household poverty at age 8 was most predictive of lower emotion regulation. Sensitive periods at ages 5 and 6 for low cognitive stimulation and accumulation of household poverty were the most predictive of adolescents’ cognitive abilities. Findings suggest that social protection and educational programs may be most effective when tailored to the types, sensitive periods, or accumulation of adversities experienced across childhood.

title: Reduced working memory offloading to unreliable artificial intelligence: Evidence from the contralateral delay activity
description: Efficient collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence (AI) systems requires a dynamic allocation of cognitive resources. Individuals must decide whether to maintain information internally or offload cognitive processing to artificial systems. Although such decisions depend critically on trust, it remains a challenge how to measure trust: existing approaches rely primarily on self-report or behavioral proxies that are indirect and often confounded by task demands. Here we tested whether the contralateral delay activity (CDA), a well-established neural marker of working memory storage, can serve as an implicit neural indicator of trust-dependent cognitive offloading. Human participants (both sexes) performed a lateralized change-detection task while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Working memory load (low, high) and interaction type (solo, reliable, unreliable AI partner) were manipulated using a repeated measures design. Participants were instructed that the AI would monitor one visual hemifield while they monitored the other, allowing them to offload memory demands depending on their trust in the AI. CDA amplitude varied systematically as a function of AI reliability and memory load. Under low working memory load, working with the reliable AI elicited larger CDA amplitudes than working with the unreliable AI, consistent with greater cognitive offloading to the automated partner. However, this effect disappeared under high memory load, suggesting that increased cognitive demands limit the extent of offloading. These findings demonstrate that the CDA provides a continuous neural index of how individuals allocate cognitive resources when interacting with artificial systems, offering a promising approach to measuring trust-related cognitive processes in human-AI collaboration.

title: Opening the Black Box of Scientific Practices – a Systematic Video Development Framework Integrating Scientific Reasoning Skills and Insights into Authentic Research Processes
description: Understanding scientific practices is fundamental to our modern society and to science education. Concepts such as Scientific Reasoning (SR) and Nature of Science (NOS) are important to operationalize different aspects of these practices. Educational policy organizations and international standards emphasize the importance of insights into the activities and thought processes of scientists to improve science learning. As the implementation of these requirements in the classroom is a challenging goal, videos are effective tools for making aspects of scientific practices visible that often remain hidden for students. Current approaches in science education tend to adopt either an affective-volitional focus by authentic insights into scientific practices or a cognitive focus by promoting student skills in the context of SR or NOS. In this theoretical contribution, we argue for a synergistic integration of these foci. Following this argument, we derive a systematic framework for video development by combining insights from science education with the contextual analysis of science and technology studies and philosophy, which aims to open the black box of scientific practices while developing videos that systematically address students' skills and provide authentic insights into scientific research processes. In this paper, we present a new systematic framework for video development and provide examples of videos created using this framework for discussion within the scientific community.

title: In the Mind or in the World? Types of Beliefs and the Locality of Evidence
description: People’s beliefs appear to be divisible into two distinct types. Some beliefs refer directly to the observable world, readily guide behavior, and are easily revised when challenged. On the other hand, ideological, political, and religious beliefs are associated with much more obscure evidence, often do not lead to behavior, and appear immune to counterevidence. To explain this intuitive difference between beliefs, several theories in psychology have proposed that the mind possesses two qualitatively different types of belief with different cognitive properties. Abelson (1986) distinguished testable from distal beliefs, where the former are updated on the evidence while the latter are held for instrumental reasons. Sperber (1997) proposed that intuitive beliefs are automatically formed by the mind, while reflective beliefs are only meta-represented, keeping them sequestered from other thoughts. Van Leeuwen (2023) divides beliefs into factual beliefs and credences, arguing that many ideological beliefs are a cognitive attitude more like imagination than true belief. In this paper, I draw on three neglected theories in psychology from the 1950s and suggest that they can explain apparent differences among beliefs without positing a novel type of belief. In so doing, I critique an assumption underlying types-of-beliefs theories: that an appeal to psychological properties is needed to explain why beliefs appear to differ from each other. In contrast, I suggest that differences among beliefs may be explained by a non-psychological characteristic of the world. This emphasis on studying the environment is inspired by Brunswik (1952, 1956). Relatedly, Bruner, Goodnow, and Austin (1956) suggested that concepts might differ not in the psychological processes used to classify them, but in the cues that contribute to their category-membership. Importing their notion of attribute immediacy to belief, I propose that beliefs differ in the locality of evidence that supports them. Whe

title: The Impact of Emotions, Flow and Addiction on Time Perception in Short Videos: An Experimental and Survey Study
description: Short-form video platforms, including TikTok, have rapidly gained popularity. Their emotionally charged, algorithm-curated content can promote addiction and distort time perception. However, there is a scarcity of research on time perception within the realm of short videos. This study aimed to explore the influence of short video emotions, individual emotions, short video addiction, and flow on time perception using experimental and survey methods. Study 1 recruited 158 participants (Mean age = 21.50 years, SD = 2.16), and employed a 2 (time estimation paradigm: prospective, retrospective) × 3 (video emotion: positive, neutral, negative) between-subjects experimental design to investigate the impact of short video emotions, time estimation paradigms, short video addiction, and flow on time perception. Findings revealed that short video emotions influenced time perception, with positive videos leading to an underestimation of duration and a faster perception of time passage. Additionally, both short video emotions and addiction predicted the perception of time passage through flow. Study 2 conducted a survey of 525 participants (Mean age = 21.53 years, SD = 2.14) and utilised structural equation modelling to explore the associations between individual emotions (depression, anxiety, boredom), short video addiction, flow, and time perception. Depression and short video addiction predicted time perception through flow, further clarifying the relationships among these variables. The findings extend the I-PACE model and flow theory to popular short-video media, highlighting the role of flow in linking emotions, addiction, and time perception during short-video use.

title: Takes one to open many: A field study assessing a representative contact Intervention
description: Intervening to improve intergroup relations is a complex and resource-intensive endeavor. Here, to promote better intergroup relations efficiently and effectively, we examine a school-based intergroup contact intervention, involving a group of (majority) group members and a representative of a minority group (i.e., representative contact). We assess this approach in a large-scale field study in 41 schools in Israel and the West Bank, in which Ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) representatives engaged in a 2-hour face-to-face discussion with groups of non-Haredi adolescents. Compared to pre-intervention levels, participants that engaged in representative contact exhibited less prejudice, more positive meta-perceptions, perceived the norms in their school to be more tolerant, and showed more willingness to learn about and engage in future meetings with Haredi group members. Our findings provide evidence from the field for the potential utility of representative contact in schools, as a cost-effective intervention to improve intergroup relations.

title: Why faster thinkers are smarter thinkers: Working memory binding as the link between processing speed and cognitive ability
description: Individuals who process information faster tend to score higher on cognitive ability tests, but the mechanism linking processing speed to general cognitive ability (g) remains unresolved. We tested whether this association is mediated by working memory capacity, and if so, whether the critical component is executive attention — as captured by complex span tasks requiring dual-task coordination and interference management — or relational binding — the ability to form and maintain temporary associations between unrelated features. In a community sample of 215 adults (aged 18–40), we measured processing speed at both the neural level (ERP component peak latencies) and the cognitive level (diffusion model drift rates), working memory through complex span and binding tasks, and g through a comprehensive cognitive ability test battery. Latent variable mediation analyses showed that complex span performance only partially mediated the speed–g relationship, leaving significant direct effects. In contrast, binding task performance fully mediated the relationship for cognitive processing speed and substantially mediated it for neural processing speed, reducing previously significant direct paths to nonsignificance. When both mediators competed in parallel models, binding emerged as the dominant predictor of g, with complex span contributing no unique variance. These findings identify relational binding as the specific working memory component that transmits the association between processing speed and cognitive ability, suggesting that the cognitive bottleneck linking processing speed to reasoning ability is not executive control but the more elemental ability to build and maintain temporary relational representations.

title: Advancing therapeutic approaches for agitation: a neurorelational perspective
description: Agitation is a common, distressing and difficult-to-treat symptom in dementia, linked to emotional dysregulation and interpersonal stress. Degenerative and compensatory changes in the locus coeruleus-noradrenergic (LC-NA) system have been implicated in agitation in Alzheimer’s disease. However, neuropathology alone does not fully explain why some individuals are more prone to agitation than others. We explore how premorbid mentalizing capacity (the ability to understand one’s own and others’ mental states) in both care recipients and caregivers may influence agitation propensity. Mentalizing, rooted in early attachment experiences, supports emotion regulation but may be compromised under stress in the context of neurodegeneration and neuropsychiatric symptoms, and this could increase the likelihood of escalation of care. We propose a neurorelational framework for understanding and addressing agitation, integrating neurobiological and socio-emotional perspectives. Targeting both care recipients’ LC-NA system and caregivers’ mentalizing capacity may represent a personalized intervention strategy to mitigate effects of neurodegeneration on ‘neuropsychiatric reserve’.

title: CATHA: A Therapist-Led Workflow for Linking Speech, Voice, and Clinical Meaning in Music Therapy
description: CATHA (Clinical Audio Translation for Therapeutic Attunement) is introduced as a therapist-guided R/Shiny methodology designed to preserve the formal aspects of voiced expression in music therapy, with particular application in oncology and palliative care settings. The method is grounded in the philosophical concept of “speech seeking orientation under finitude,” which posits that speech in the context of serious illness not only conveys symptoms, preferences, or beliefs, but also seeks orientation, relational connection, containment, and a livable position within altered life circumstances. The accompanying philosophical manuscript contends that such speech is conveyed not only through semantic content but also through pacing, contour, hesitation, silence, recurrence, breath, and reaction, and that music therapy is uniquely positioned to address these expressive modalities. CATHA translates this insight into a transparent mixed-methods workflow comprising audio processing, waveform inspection, therapist-defined segmentation, acoustic feature extraction, score-like contour rendering, and uncertainty marking. The method is not intended as an emotion-recognition system, diagnostic tool, or predictor of clinical outcomes. Rather, CATHA serves as a methodological prototype for integrating transcript, vocal form, therapist interpretation, and reproducible research artefacts. This method's paper outlines the conceptual foundation, implementation logic, intended application in music therapy, validation strategy, and ethical considerations of CATHA. CATHA is available as an R/Shiny prototype (https://github.com/sgjerga/CATHA) and as an online application (https://sgjerga-catha.share.connect.posit.cloud/).

title: From Wounded Healers to Commercialized Caregivers: A Scoping Review of Mental Health Content Creators on Social Media
description: An increasing number of content creators, including clinicians and people with lived experiences, are sharing mental health–related content on social media. This review maps the empirical literature on mental health content creators, with the aim of synthesizing evidence on motivations for content creation and engagement, communicative practices, and associated outcomes for both creators and their audiences. In addition, it advances a working definition of mental health content creators that integrates and extends definitions identified in the literature. The search across nine databases identified 59 peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2025, examining a wide range of platforms, most commonly YouTube (35.6%), TikTok (23.7%), and Instagram (20.3%). Most studies focused on content creators with lived experience of mental disorders (81.4%), whereas only a small minority examined those with professional expertise (8.5%). Beyond mental health conditions in general terms (32.2%), the most frequently shared topics were neurodevelopmental disorders (15.3%), feeding and eating disorders (13.6%), and depressive disorders (10.2%). Communicative practices were investigated across four domains: psychoeducation (addressed in 66.1% of studies), service promotion (5.1%), self-disclosure (47.5% reported positive framings; 47.5% reported negative framings), and advocacy (30.5%). The included studies reported a wide range of motivations for content creation, spanning from altruistic intentions to help others to self-validation. Motivations underlying audience engagement remained comparatively underexplored. Across studies, findings reveal persistent tensions between platformed care and commerce, highlighting how platform logics such as algorithmic visibility shape disclosure practices and audience engagement. title: Affective Measures for Italian (AMI): Valence, Arousal and Dominance Norms for 13,495 Italian Nouns, Adjective and Verbs
description:
Words affective properties influence a broad range of cognitive processes and should be carefully considered when selecting verbal stimuli for experimental tasks. Although large-scale affective norm databases are available in several languages, Italian still lacks such an extensive resource. This limitation is relevant given the rich inflectional structure of Italian, which offers unique opportunities to investigate how morpho-syntactic variations may shape words affective processing.
To address this gap, we present a large-scale database collecting ratings of valence, arousal, and dominance for 13,495 Italian words, including three major parts of speech (PoS): nouns, adjectives, and verbs. Singular forms were included for nouns; masculine and feminine singular forms for adjectives; and, for verbs, infinitives together with first- and third-person singular present-tense forms of the indicative mood. 
Analyses showed that the distribution patterns of Italian affective ratings are largely consistent with those reported in previous affective norming studies. The relationship among the affective dimensions displayed the typical structure observed in the literature: valence and dominance showed a strong positive linear association, whereas arousal displayed significant quadratic U-shaped relationships with both valence and dominance, highlighting higher activation for words receiving extreme ratings in valence and dominance. These patterns were substantially replicated across grammatical classes.
The present dataset expands previous affective resources available for Italian and provides a reliable tool for psycholinguistic, cognitive, and cross-linguistic investigations. Crucially, the inclusion of multiple PoS and morphological forms makes this dataset particularly suitable for exploring how lexical and grammatical properties contribute to affective word processing.

title: Serial Dependence Scales with Action-binding Depth in Duration Perception
description: Serial dependence biases perception toward recent history, yet it often appears only when observers respond actively. The critical issue, however, is whether the effect depends on motor output itself or on how strongly stimulus features are built into the response plan. We tested this by comparing active duration reproduction with passive following, where observers simply tracked stimulus onset and offset with a sustained keypress. Twenty-four participants completed both tasks with physically matched sensory input, equating stimulus properties and motor execution, while the degree of coupling between duration and action varied. The sequential bias was strongest for reproduction-after-reproduction trials, weaker for reproduction-after-following trials, and minimal when the current trial required following. Passive following still showed central tendency, with offset latency revealing implicit duration encoding, but it generated little attraction across trials. These findings point to action-binding depth, rather than motor output alone, as the key driver of serial dependence in time perception.

title: Feedback anticipation and integration in risk preferences from childhood to elderhood
description: Risk preferences are shaped by outcome anticipation and feedback integration. Understanding how these processes evolve across the human lifespan is essential for theoretical models of decision-making, for applications in education, and behavioral public policy aimed at protecting against age-related vulnerabilities. This study examines the lifespan development (N = 658; ages 8 to 78) of decision-making under risk through the lens of these two constitutive components, using a behavioral paradigm merging descriptive and experiential information. Our findings replicate the established pattern of a peak of risk-taking during adolescence, followed by a steady decline with aging. Moreover, our results show that while the influence of outcome anticipation matures gradually during childhood and adolescence, the propensity to learn from feedback diminishes progressively with age. These results suggest that while adults may rely on more sophisticated internal models of probability, these models may paradoxically support faulty reasoning, potentially contributing to suboptimal choices.

title: Memorability as an Emergent Property: How Representational Structure Creates Apparent Intrinsic Effects
description: Some pictures, videos, faces, voices, and words are reliably remembered better than others, a phenomenon known as memorability. This has been widely interpreted as reflecting a stable, intrinsic property of the stimuli themselves. Here we argue that this consistency is better explained by the relational structure of the stimulus sets used to measure memorability, rather than as an intrinsic property of the items. Using simulations with a global matching model of recognition memory, we show that apparent intrinsic memorability emerges naturally from distinctiveness — how dissimilar an item is from others in a given set of encoded images — without any stimulus-intrinsic mechanism. In behavioral experiments, we demonstrate that manipulating the similarity structure of image sets can invert memorability rankings, making previously memorable images forgettable and vice versa. We also show that features previously identified as intrinsically memorable (such as “body-part related”) are the most representationally distinctive features in standard databases, explaining their memorability. To address these large variations in distinctiveness we created a new image set that reduced variability in representational distinctiveness, and found it significantly diminishes all feature-memorability relationships. These findings suggest that memorability is not a fixed attribute of items themselves, but an emergent property of which items are distinctive within the context, with implications for how we attribute stable psychological properties to stimuli more broadly.

title: Evaluating User Perspective on a Mindfulness Based- Intervention for Improving Risk and Protective Factors of Disordered Eating: A Person- Based Approach.
description:
Objective: This study aimed to evaluate a brief  digital mindfulness intervention designed to target body image and eating disorder risk factors among young adults aged 16-34, as part of a wider mixed methods research taking a person-based approach during the development of a digital mindfulness-based intervention.
Method: A person-based approach was used involving think-aloud interviews and semi-structured interviews with 10 participants (5 Male, 5 Female) (mean age=26.5, SD=5.68)  without current eating disorders. Reflexive thematic analysis was conducted following Braun and Clarke's (2006) six-phase approach.
Results: Three main themes emerged - usability, acceptability, and feasibility of the tailored mindfulness program. Participants found the content clear, simple, coherent and engaging. They reported increased self-awareness and more adaptive thought patterns, indicating acceptability. All participants intended to continue practicing the techniques, reflecting feasibility. However, participants also mentioned practical challenges in maintaining focus during the mindfulness practices. The table of changes created after the first set of interviews allowed incorporation of modifications to address issues like reducing long pauses and adding more guidance during exercises based on initial user feedback.
Discussion: While an expanded trial is warranted, findings provide initial evidence that accessible, tailored digital mindfulness tools can successfully engage youth and cultivate protective skills relevant to body image and disordered eating prevention. Further research into optimized blended digital mindfulness interventions is needed as an engaging early prevention approach for escalating mental health risks among young people. The digital format enables scalable delivery on platforms youth already access.
Keywords: digital mindfulness-based intervention, person- based approach, disordered eating, young adults, prevention.

title: The Cannabis Research Image Database (CRESIDA): a standardized and validated image set for studying cannabis cue-reactivity
description: Background and Aims: Cannabis cue-reactivity paradigms are instrumental in studying the behavioral and neurocognitive mechanisms of cannabis use and cannabis use disorders. However, image sets used for cannabis cue-reactivity paradigms vary between studies, and the lack of reliability and validity assessment hinders the quality of evidence they generate. The main aim of this study was to create a novel, open access, standardized, and representative database of cannabis use-related images including control images matched by resolution, luminosity, and complexity: The Cannabis Research Image Database (CRESIDA). The secondary aim was to examine whether subjective cannabis cue-induced craving was associated with cannabis‑use severity and whether this relationship was moderated by image type. As an illustrative example of how our open data can be used and how sample characteristics can shape cue‑reactivity, we also explored the role of cannabis–tobacco mixing by comparing cannabis cue-induced cannabis and tobacco craving between individuals who did and did not mix the substances. Design: An online survey was administered to participants recruited via online platforms, community advertisement, and snowballing. Setting: USA, the Netherlands, and Australia. Participants/Cases: 689 participants who consumed cannabis monthly-to-daily (385 men, 298 women, 6 other) were recruited between January 2022 and May 2024. Measurements: Out of 93 cannabis images and 93 matched neutral images, participants each rated 31 image pairs for cannabis craving (the primary outcome), arousal, valence, and tobacco craving. Participants were characterized for socio-demographic data, level of cannabis use and related problems, and mixing cannabis and tobacco. A subset of 78 images was selected for further analysis based on cannabis craving results. Image ratings were evaluated for internal consistency (). Furthermore, we examined the association between cannabis cravings and cannabis use characteri

title: Within-person prospective associations between youth psychopathology and white matter development and the moderating role of parental mental health
description:
Background: Adolescence is a developmental period involving ongoing white matter (WM) maturation and rising risk for psychopathology. This risk is particularly elevated among youth whose parents have mental health problems. 
Methods: Leveraging longitudinal data from three waves of the community-based Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (N = 6,581, Nobservations = 16, 271, mean ageTP 1 = 10.2, mean ageTP 2 = 12.0 , mean ageTP 3 = 14.2), we employed random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs) to disentangle stable between-person differences from time-varying within-person changes. We examined prospective and bidirectional associations between youth general psychopathology and diffusion metrics, including fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) in the uncinate fasciculus (UF), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), and corpus callosum (CC). We also tested whether parental psychopathology moderated these associations. 
Results: Preregistered analyses showed no significant between-person or within-person associations between parent-reported youth psychopathology and WM microstructure, nor evidence of moderation by parental psychopathology. In exploratory analyses using youth self-reports, SLF and CC FA were negatively associated with psychopathology at the between-person level, but positively associated at the within-person level during early adolescence. Additionally, SLF and CC MD were negatively associated with self-reported psychopathology on the within-person level during early adolescence, with this association persisting into mid-adolescence for the CC. Parental psychopathology moderated the within-person association between CC MD and self-reported youth psychopathology.
